resources.label: Learn C#
resources.note: Our C# practice site. Type each example in, run it, and change it. C# is one of the languages AQA accepts in the exam.

tips.title: FOR knows the count, WHILE does not
tips.body: Use **FOR** when you know how many times in advance, which is definite iteration. Use **WHILE** when you are waiting for a condition, which is indefinite. That one distinction answers most of the vocabulary questions.

tips.title: WHILE tests before, REPEAT tests after
tips.body: A `WHILE` loop can run **zero** times, because the condition is checked first. A `REPEAT UNTIL` always runs **at least once**. Questions are set on exactly that difference.

tips.title: Trace one row past the end
tips.body: When tracing a loop, work out the pass where the condition finally fails and write that row down. Stopping one row early is the commonest tracing error, and it changes the final value.

tips.title: Inner loop runs fully each time
tips.body: In a nested pair, the inner loop completes **every** time the outer loop goes round once. An outer loop of 3 with an inner of 4 runs the inner body $3 \times 4 = 12$ times.

steps.title: Selection: IF, ELSE IF, ELSE
steps.body:
**Selection** chooses between paths. AQA pseudo-code:

```
IF mark ≥ 70 THEN
   OUTPUT 'A'
ELSE IF mark ≥ 50 THEN
   OUTPUT 'B'
ELSE
   OUTPUT 'C'
ENDIF
```

The conditions are tested **in order**, and **only the first True branch runs**; the rest are skipped, even if they would also be True. So a mark of 85 outputs `A` only, never `B` as well. The order therefore matters: test the most demanding condition first.

**Nested** selection is an IF inside an IF. It is easiest to trace by indenting, and by remembering that the inner IF is only reached when the outer condition was True.

props.title: Only the first True branch runs

visuals.alt: A trace of the grade selection for four marks, showing which branch runs

visuals.problem: Trace this nested IF with `age ← 15` and `ticket ← 'no'`

steps.text:
```
IF age ≥ 13 THEN
   IF ticket = 'yes' THEN
      OUTPUT 'Enter'
   ELSE
      OUTPUT 'Buy a ticket'
   ENDIF
ELSE
   OUTPUT 'Too young'
ENDIF
```
Outer test: `15 ≥ 13` is True, so the outer ELSE is skipped completely
steps.note: the outer condition picks the half

steps.text: Only now is the inner IF reached at all
steps.note: an inner IF runs only when the outer test was True

steps.text: Inner test: `'no' = 'yes'` is False, so the inner ELSE runs
Output: `Buy a ticket`, and nothing else. With `age ← 11` the outer test fails, `Too young` is output and the inner IF is never tested

check.prompt: What is output by the grade code above when `mark` is 50?
check.solution: 50 is not ≥ 70, but it **is** ≥ 50: **B**. Boundaries belong to the ≥ side.

steps.title: Definite iteration: FOR
steps.body:
A **FOR** loop repeats a **known** number of times, counting with a variable:

```
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 5
   total ← total + i
ENDFOR
```

Both limits are **included**: i takes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, so the body runs five times. The number of passes from a to b is $b - a + 1$.

**STEP** changes the count: `FOR i ← 2 TO 10 STEP 4` gives 2, 6, 10. A negative step counts down: `FOR i ← 3 TO 1 STEP -1` gives 3, 2, 1.

AQA also allows `FOR item IN list … ENDFOR` to visit every element of an array, and `FOR char IN text` to walk a string. Array items cannot be changed that way, so use the indexed loop when you need to write to the array.

visuals.alt: A trace table of a FOR loop adding 1 to 5 into total

check.prompt: How many times does `FOR i ← 0 TO 9` run its body?

steps.title: Indefinite iteration: WHILE and REPEAT UNTIL
steps.body:
When you do not know how many times, the loop runs **until something changes**: **indefinite** iteration.

**WHILE** tests **before** each pass and continues while the condition is True:

```
n ← 1
WHILE n < 20
   n ← n * 3
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT n
```

n goes 1, 3, 9, 27; at 27 the test fails and the loop stops. If the condition is False at the start, the body never runs.

**REPEAT … UNTIL** tests **after** each pass and stops when the condition becomes True:

```
count ← 0
REPEAT
   count ← count + 2
UNTIL count ≥ 7
```

The body always runs **at least once**, which makes REPEAT the natural loop for *ask, then check*: input validation and password attempts.

visuals.alt: A table contrasting WHILE and REPEAT UNTIL loops

visuals.problem: Trace `count ← 0`, then `REPEAT count ← count + 2 UNTIL count ≥ 7`

steps.text: Pass 1: count becomes 2, then the test `2 ≥ 7` is False, so go round again
steps.note: the test comes after the body

steps.text: Pass 4: count becomes 8; `8 ≥ 7` is True, so the loop ends with count = 8
steps.note: UNTIL stops when the condition becomes True

steps.text: The loop overshoots 7, because UNTIL cannot stop part-way through a pass
steps.note: a WHILE would test before adding

check.prompt: A WHILE loop's condition is False the first time it is tested. How many times does the body run?
check.solution: WHILE tests first, so a False condition means the body is skipped entirely: **0**.
options: It depends on the body
Infinitely

steps.title: Tracing: one column per variable, one row per change
steps.body: A **trace table** is how the exam tests loops. Columns for every variable, plus the condition and the output; a new row each time something changes. Never skip a row, even when a value repeats.

visuals.alt: A trace table for the WHILE loop n ← n * 3 while n < 20

steps.text: Row 1: n is 1, the test is True, so the body runs and n becomes 3
Rows 2 and 3: still True at 3 and 9
Row 4: n is 27, the test is False, the loop stops; OUTPUT n prints 27
steps.note: the value that fails the test is the one output

check.prompt: Using the same loop but starting with `n ← 2`, what is output?

steps.title: Nested loops
steps.body:
A loop inside a loop: the **inner** loop runs completely for **each** pass of the outer one.

```
FOR i ← 1 TO 2
   FOR j ← 1 TO 3
      OUTPUT i * j
   ENDFOR
ENDFOR
```

The outer loop runs 2 times and the inner 3 times each, so the body runs $2 \times 3 = 6$ times, outputting 1, 2, 3, then 2, 4, 6. The inner counter resets to 1 every time the outer counter moves on.

In a trace table give the inner counter its own column and watch it restart. The commonest slip is to run the inner loop only once.

props.title: Nested loops: the inner one restarts

visuals.alt: A trace table of two nested FOR loops outputting i times j

check.prompt:
How many times does the body run?

```
FOR i ← 1 TO 4
   FOR j ← 1 TO 5
      count ← count + 1
   ENDFOR
ENDFOR
```

steps.title: The errors loops invite
steps.body:
Three logic errors account for most lost marks.

**Off-by-one.** `WHILE i < 10` stops before 10; `FOR i ← 1 TO 10` includes it. Decide whether the limit is meant to be included, then choose `<` or `≤`, and check the first and last values in a trace.

**The infinite loop.** A WHILE whose condition can never become False, usually because the body forgets to change the variable in the condition: `WHILE n < 20` with no line that changes n. In a trace it shows as a column that never moves.

**The inverted condition.** `UNTIL valid = False` when the loop should stop once the input is valid. Say the condition out loud: REPEAT *until* it is right.

All three are **logic errors** in AQA's terms: the code runs, but does the wrong thing. A **syntax error** would be a missing ENDFOR, which stops it running at all.

rows: one value too few or too many
change the loop variable inside the body
stops at the wrong time, or never

What is wrong here?

```
n ← 1
```

steps.title: Your turn: trace it
steps.body:
Trace this program in a table with columns for x, the condition and the output, then reveal. Count the rows: the number of times the body ran is one fewer than the number of times the condition was tested.

```
x ← 10
WHILE x > 3
   x ← x - 4
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT x
```

Then build the same loop on our [Learn C#](https://red-dune-0f7372e10.7.azurestaticapps.net/) site as a `while`, with a `Console.WriteLine(x)` inside it, and check the values it prints against the rows of your table.

visuals.alt: A trace table for x ← x − 4 while x > 3, starting from 10

check.prompt: Same loop, but starting with `x ← 15`. What is output?

steps.title: Going deeper: choose the loop, convert between loops, explain the purpose
steps.body:
**Choose the loop from the problem.** A known count (10 inputs, every array element): FOR. Until a limit is reached: WHILE. Ask then check: REPEAT UNTIL. Saying *why* is a mark.

**Convert between them.** Any FOR is a WHILE with a counter you manage yourself: initialise before, test at the top, increment at the bottom. Exams ask for this to see whether you understand what FOR hides.

**Trace with a condition column.** Write the test result every time; the row where it flips is where the marks are.

**Explain what an algorithm does.** Read the loop, find what changes, find what stops it, then say the purpose in one sentence: *counts the odd numbers from 1 to 9*, *finds the largest of ten inputs*, *allows three password attempts*.

**Write algorithms with the structure closed.** ENDIF, ENDFOR, ENDWHILE, and the output **after** the loop, not inside it.

check.prompt: Which loop is best for *keep asking for a number until it is between 1 and 10*?
check.solution: Ask, then check: **REPEAT … UNTIL**. A FOR would run a fixed number of times, which is not what is wanted.
options: REPEAT … UNTIL, because it asks first and checks after
FOR, because the numbers run from 1 to 10
WHILE, because the number is known before the first ask
IF, because the number is checked against the range

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Selection**: IF … ELSE IF … ELSE … ENDIF; conditions tested in order, only the first True branch runs.
- **FOR** (definite): both limits included, $b - a + 1$ passes; STEP for other counts; FOR … IN for arrays.
- **WHILE** tests before, may run zero times; **REPEAT … UNTIL** tests after, runs at least once and stops when the condition becomes True.
- **Nested loops**: the inner loop runs fully for each outer pass; passes multiply.
- **Trace tables**: a column per variable plus the condition and output; a row per change; the value that fails the test is the one left.
- **Errors**: off-by-one, infinite loop, inverted condition; all logic errors.
- **Choose and convert**: FOR for a known count, WHILE for a limit, REPEAT for ask-then-check; any FOR can be written as a WHILE.

visuals.alt: A summary table of the three loops with their test timing and minimum passes

questions.prompt:
What is output?

```
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 5
   total ← total + i
ENDFOR
OUTPUT total
```
questions.solution: The loop runs for i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (both limits included) and adds each: $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = $ **15**.

questions.prompt:
How many times does the loop body run?

```
FOR i ← 3 TO 7
   OUTPUT i
ENDFOR
```
questions.solution: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7: **5** times. AQA FOR loops include both limits, so the count is $7 - 3 + 1$.

questions.prompt:
What is output when `mark` is 69?

```
IF mark ≥ 70 THEN
   OUTPUT 'A'
ELSE IF mark ≥ 50 THEN
   OUTPUT 'B'
ELSE
   OUTPUT 'C'
ENDIF
```
questions.solution: 69 is not ≥ 70, so the first branch is skipped. 69 is ≥ 50, so **B**. Only one branch of an IF–ELSE IF–ELSE ever runs.

questions.prompt: Which loop keeps going while a condition is True and checks it **before** each pass?
questions.solution: A **WHILE** loop tests its condition first, so its body may run zero times. REPEAT … UNTIL tests afterwards and always runs at least once. FOR counts.
options: WHILE … ENDWHILE
REPEAT … UNTIL
FOR … ENDFOR
IF … ENDIF

questions.prompt:
What is output?

```
n ← 1
WHILE n < 20
   n ← n * 3
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT n
```
questions.solution: n goes 1 → 3 → 9 → 27. At 27 the condition `n < 20` is False, so the loop stops and **27** is output. The loop overshoots the limit: that is normal, and a trace table shows it.

questions.prompt:
What is output?

```
count ← 0
REPEAT
   count ← count + 2
UNTIL count ≥ 7
OUTPUT count
```
questions.solution: count: 2, 4, 6, 8. After 8 the condition `count ≥ 7` is True, so the loop ends: **8**. UNTIL stops when the condition becomes True.

questions.prompt:
How many times is `total ← total + 1` executed?

```
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 3
   FOR j ← 1 TO 2
      total ← total + 1
   ENDFOR
ENDFOR
```
questions.solution: The inner loop runs twice for **each** of the three outer passes: $3 \times 2 = $ **6**.

questions.prompt:
What is output?

```
FOR i ← 2 TO 10 STEP 4
   OUTPUT i
ENDFOR
```
questions.solution: STEP 4 adds 4 each time: **2, 6, 10**. 14 would pass the limit, so it is not output.
**Definite** iteration repeats a known number of times: a FOR loop. **Indefinite** iteration repeats until a condition changes: WHILE and REPEAT … UNTIL.
options: A FOR loop that runs a set number of times
A WHILE loop that runs until the user types 'stop'
A REPEAT loop that runs until a password is correct
An IF statement that runs once

questions.prompt:
What is output?

```
count ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 9
   IF i MOD 2 = 1 THEN
      count ← count + 1
   ENDIF
ENDFOR
OUTPUT count
```
questions.solution: `i MOD 2 = 1` is True for the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9: **5** of them.

questions.prompt:
What is output?

```
x ← 10
WHILE x > 3
   x ← x - 4
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT x
```
questions.skill: tracing a WHILE loop past its limit
questions.solution: x: 10 → 6 → 2. When x is 2 the condition `x > 3` is False: **2**. Note the loop runs twice, not until x is 3.

questions.prompt:
What is output?

```
n ← 5
REPEAT
   n ← n - 1
   OUTPUT n
UNTIL n = 2
```
questions.skill: tracing REPEAT UNTIL with output inside
questions.solution: n becomes 4 and is output; then 3; then 2, output, and now `n = 2` is True so the loop ends: **4, 3, 2**.

questions.prompt: Write pseudo-code that inputs 10 numbers and outputs the largest.
questions.skill: writing an algorithm with a loop
questions.solution: A FOR loop of 10 inputs, each converted with STRING_TO_INT, a `largest` variable initialised from the first input, an IF that replaces it when a bigger number arrives, and one OUTPUT after the loop.

markScheme.description: a loop that reads 10 numbers in total, for example one input before `FOR i ← 2 TO 10`
input converted with STRING_TO_INT inside the loop
largest initialised sensibly, e.g. to the first number
IF number > largest THEN largest ← number
OUTPUT largest after the loop, not inside it

criteria.text: A loop that reads 10 numbers in total, for example one input before `FOR i ← 2 TO 10`
Each number input and converted to an integer
largest initialised, for example from the first input
IF number > largest THEN largest ← number
OUTPUT largest once, after the loop

questions.modelAnswer:
largest ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
FOR i ← 2 TO 10
   number ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
   IF number > largest THEN
      largest ← number
   ENDIF
ENDFOR
OUTPUT largest

questions.prompt:
This loop is meant to output the numbers 1 to 10 but outputs 1 to 9. What is the error called, and what is the fix?

```
i ← 1
WHILE i < 10
   OUTPUT i
   i ← i + 1
ENDWHILE
```
questions.solution: The loop stops when i reaches 10, so 10 is never output: an **off-by-one** error, the commonest logic error in loops. `i ≤ 10` includes it.
options: An off-by-one error; change the condition to i ≤ 10
A syntax error; change WHILE to FOR
An off-by-one error; start i at 0
A logic error; move OUTPUT after i ← i + 1

questions.prompt:
What is output?

```
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 4
   total ← total + i * i
ENDFOR
OUTPUT total
```
questions.solution: $1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = $ **30**: the squares of 1 to 4. A trace table with columns i, i * i and total keeps it straight.

questions.prompt:
Explain what this algorithm does, and state the value of `tries` when it ends if the user's second entry is correct.

```
tries ← 0
REPEAT
   entry ← USERINPUT
   tries ← tries + 1
UNTIL entry = 'open' OR tries = 3
```
questions.skill: explaining the purpose of an algorithm
questions.solution: It asks for a password until either the right word is entered or three attempts have been used, whichever comes first. If the second entry is 'open', tries is **2** when the loop ends.

markScheme.description: repeatedly reads an entry and counts the attempts
stops when the entry is 'open' or after 3 attempts, whichever first

criteria.text: Stops on the correct entry or after three attempts

questions.modelAnswer: The algorithm keeps reading an entry and counting the attempts. It stops as soon as the entry is 'open', or when three attempts have been made, whichever happens first: it is a password check with a limit of three tries. If the second entry is 'open', the loop ends with tries equal to 2.

questions.prompt: Which loop runs its body at least once, whatever the condition?
questions.solution: **REPEAT … UNTIL** tests its condition at the end, so the body has already run once. A WHILE with a false condition runs zero times, and FOR 5 TO 1 without a negative STEP runs zero times.
options: REPEAT … UNTIL
WHILE … ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 5 TO 1
IF … ELSE

questions.prompt:
Trace the nested loops. What is the **last** value output?

```
FOR i ← 1 TO 2
   FOR j ← 1 TO 3
      OUTPUT i * j
   ENDFOR
ENDFOR
```

examTechnique.body:
Paper 1 tests iteration and selection almost entirely through tracing and writing. For tracing, draw the table before you start: one column per variable, a column for the condition, a column for output, and a row every time a value changes. Include the row where the condition fails, because the value in that row is usually the answer. For nested loops give the inner counter its own column and let it restart.

For writing, choose the loop from the problem and say why if asked, keep the output outside the loop when a single result is wanted, and close every structure. Check boundaries: FOR includes both limits, WHILE with < excludes the limit. When a question asks what an algorithm does, name its purpose in one sentence rather than narrating the lines.
examinerErrors: Tracing a WHILE loop as if it stopped exactly at the limit rather than at the first value that fails the test.
Running the inner loop of a nested pair only once.
Off-by-one errors: WHILE i < 10 when 10 should be included.
Putting OUTPUT inside the loop when the question wants a single final result.
Using a FOR loop for a task that repeats until a condition, such as a password check.
Leaving ENDIF, ENDFOR or ENDWHILE out of written pseudo-code.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer traces any loop, nested or not, in a complete table with a condition column, and reads off the value that stops the loop. It writes algorithms with the right loop for the task, the structures closed and the output placed correctly, converts a FOR to a WHILE, and describes the purpose of an unfamiliar algorithm in a sentence. It names loop errors as logic errors and fixes off-by-one boundaries deliberately.
